input.title: HoloSplat: Real-Time Token Streaming for Feed-Forward Human Reconstruction
input.comment: 43 pages including supplementary material, 20 figures. Project page: https://heaticy.github.io/HoloSplat/
input.summary: Live free-viewpoint video streaming of humans enables immersive telepresence and interactive XR applications. However, this requires reconstructing each frame in real time, transmitting the data within strict bandwidth budgets, and decoding it on lightweight client GPUs. Existing approaches, whether relying on per-frame optimization or feed-forward inference, generate massive 3D Gaussian payloads that exceed practical streaming limits, while aggressive compression severely degrades rendering quality. In this work, we present HoloSplat, a real-time streaming framework for human-centric volumetric video. HoloSplat splits a feed-forward reconstructor before its Gaussian head, introducing a multi-rate streaming codec driven by server-side token compression and client-side token restoration. On the server side, we apply opacity-guided token pruning, PCA-based dimensionality reduction, and lossless geometry coding for token anchors. On the client side, a feature reconstruction hypernetwork is fused into the Gaussian head to recover compression-induced quality loss. Furthermore, we introduce Neural Session Calibration (NSC), which rapidly fine-tunes the Gaussian head online using incoming camera views during a warm-up phase. This resolves quality degradation from novel camera parameters and varying capture conditions with zero per-frame overhead. In our evaluations, HoloSplat averages 32.2 FPS on four RTX 5090 GPUs at 50 Mbit/s. It decodes each frame into 3D Gaussians in 22.1 ms on an RTX 3050 Ti laptop GPU, transmitting 22.8$\times$ less data than uncompressed float32 Gaussians, while calibrated decoding improves PSNR by 1.050 dB.

input.title: Graph2Scene: Relation-Aware Text-to-Image Generation with Graph-Guided Diffusion Model
input.summary: Text-to-image diffusion models still struggle with complex prompts containing many elements and interactions. Existing attention-control methods mainly focus on controlling where elements appear, but often ignore how objects interact with each other. As a result, relation tokens describing interactions between elements may assign high attention to irrelevant regions, leading to missing or incorrect interactions. In this paper, we propose Graph2Scene, a training-free framework that treats scene graphs as a core control signal for diffusion generation. It represents elements as nodes and their relations as edges, and translates these element-relation dependencies into selective attention guidance. It grounds each element to its corresponding region and guides relational interactions among the involved elements. To achieve appropriate relation control without over-constraining the generation process, Graph2Scene further adapts the control duration to scene complexity and progressively relaxes graph guidance during denoising. Experiments on T2I-CompBench and ConceptMix show clear improvements in compositional generation, especially for object relations. On ConceptMix, Graph2Scene improves relationship accuracy from 0.59 to 0.84 over the strongest FLUX.1-based regional-control baseline. Results on LongBench-T2I further show its advantage on long and complex prompts.

input.title: A High-Resolution UAV Benchmark Dataset and Baseline Evaluation for Teak Crown Segmentation in Western Ghats Tropical Forests
input.summary: Accurate teak-tree segmentation from high-resolution drone imagery is critical for sustainable plantation management, yet lacks dedicated benchmarks. We introduce TeakTreeNet, a comprehensive dataset and evaluation protocol for binary teak-tree segmentation at native 2cm resolution. Four state-of-the-art architectures: U-Net, PSPNet, DeepLabV3, and SegFormer were rigorously benchmarked across scratch and ImageNet-pretrained settings with three-seed reproducibility. SegFormer establishes new SOTA performance with F1 0.938 +/- 0.002 (Teak), IoU 0.968 +/- 0.001 (Teak), and Accuracy 0.986 +/- 0.001, outperforming all pretrained CNNs. Domain-adaptive training suffices, as the scratch SegFormer outperforms ImageNet pretrained baselines, avoiding large-scale pretraining overhead. Comprehensive analysis reveals Transformer's superior boundary delineation for dense plantation scenarios. TeakTreeNet provides researchers with 6391 expertly annotated drone patches (224x224) and establishes reproducible evaluation protocols, enabling direct comparison of future methods. Our benchmark demonstrates SegFormer's optimal balance of accuracy, efficiency, and deployability for operational forestry monitoring of teak plantations for India's western tropical forests.

input.title: Learning Dense Head-Object Contact Estimation with Synthetic Data
input.summary: Head serves a critical role in human cognitive and perceptual functions while remaining vulnerable to external impacts, making the understanding of head contact essential for human safety. Despite its importance, dense head-object contact estimation remains largely unexplored, primarily due to the absence of head-object contact data. Recently, it has been shown that synthetic data can serve as powerful training data in limited data scenario, implying the potential of synthetic data in head-object contact estimation. There are two core challenges for dense head-object contact estimation. First, head-object interactions are highly diverse, resulting in substantial variations in contact regions and patterns across different objects and interaction types. Second, head contact regions are often heavily occluded by hair, making direct visual observation of the actual contact regions difficult. To address these issues, we introduce HEad COntact estimation (HECO) with synthetic data. To handle diverse head-object interactions, we leverage semantic context from text features that encode semantic relationships between head regions and interacting objects. To resolve hair occlusion issue of actual head contact regions, we introduce occlusion-aware contact learning that learns to infer head contact beyond visible information from images via amodal inpainting. As a result, we enable head-object contact estimation with HECO trained with our synthetic dataset, overcoming the issue of absence of contact data. The codes will be released.

input.title: GSDet: Gaussian Splatting for Oriented Object Detection
input.summary: Oriented object detection has advanced with the development of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and transformers. However, modern detectors still rely on predefined object candidates, such as anchors in CNN-based methods or queries in transformer-based methods, which struggle to capture spatial information effectively. To address the limitations, we propose GSDet, a novel framework that formulates oriented object detection as Gaussian splatting. Specifically, our approach performs detection within a 3D feature space constructed from image features, where 3D Gaussians are employed to represent oriented objects. These 3D Gaussians are projected onto the image plane to form 2D Gaussians, which are then transformed into oriented boxes. Furthermore, we optimize the mean, anisotropic covariance, and confidence scores of these randomly initialized 3D Gaussians, using a decoder that incorporates 3D Gaussian sampling. Moreover, our method exhibits flexibility, enabling adaptive control and a dynamic number of Gaussians during inference. Experiments on 3 datasets indicate that GSDet achieves AP$_{50}$ gains of 0.7\% on DIOR-R, 0.3\% on DOTA-v1.0, and 0.55\% on DOTA-v1.5 when evaluated with adaptive control and outperforms mainstream detectors.

input.title: DARE: Dual-Level Adversarial Learning with Domain-Aware Regularization for Whole Slide Image Classification
input.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 22 pages, 7 figures, including the appendix
input.summary: Pathological whole slide images (WSIs) exhibit substantial domain shifts across hospitals due to variations in scanning devices, staining protocols, and tissue preparation procedures, leading to significant performance degradation when models are applied to data from different sources. Although unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) has shown strong performance in transferring models from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain in natural images, it remains relatively underexplored in computational pathology. The ultra-high resolution of WSIs and their pronounced inter-slide and intra-slide heterogeneity pose unique challenges for domain adaptation, often rendering existing UDA methods unstable and susceptible to negative transfer. To address these challenges, we propose Dual-level Adversarial learning with domain-aware REgularization (DARE), a plug-and-play UDA framework for WSI classification. DARE incorporates adaptive pseudo-labeling within a teacher-student architecture to provide stable supervision for the target domain, alongside adversarial alignment of both patch-level and slide-level embeddings. Together, these components enable the joint optimization of semantic representations at both levels for cross-domain alignment. We further introduce domain-aware attention masking to regularize attention and improve cross-domain generalization. Extensive experiments on four public WSI datasets demonstrate that DARE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across various domain shifts.

input.title: Foundation Model and Radiomics Distance Scores for Post-Hoc Segmentation Failure Detection
input.comment: Accepted at the UNSURE MICCAI 2026 Workshop
input.summary: Medical image segmentation models can fail silently when clinical data differs from training data. Deployed models rarely ship with quality control, and are often black boxes. Prior methods that work in this post-hoc failure detection setting still need a separate regression or segmentation model, registration, or access to model internals. We instead propose two failure scores based on the Mahalanobis distance to a labeled reference set. The first uses radiomic shape features of the predicted mask. The second uses frozen foundation model (FM) features, made mask-aware by overlaying the mask on the image, encoding it with a frozen DINOv3, and pooling patch features with more weight on the mask region. We test on multi-site prostate and hippocampus MRI under imaging-protocol and population shift. Ranking cases by predicted failure risk within each site, both scores are competitive with the registration-based (Atlas-RCA) and ensemble-based (pairwise Dice) baselines, without registration that can fail silently or access to individual predictions. Our results show that pooling all test cases into one ranking, as prior work does, rewards ordering sites by difficulty, so a detector can rank sites well, miss failures within them, and still look strong. input.summary: Proactive streaming video understanding requires models to interpret unfolding events, respond timely, and retrieve relevant historical evidence. To systematically evaluate these capabilities, we introduce SVUBench, a comprehensive proactive streaming video benchmark comprising 12,131 questions and 62,881 answer points across ten proactive tasks spanning Perception, Understanding, and Reasoning. Constructed through model-assisted annotation and human verification, SVUBench introduces two complementary interaction modes. Basic evaluates sustained proactive responses from video onset, while Trajectory requires historical recovery and continuous response updates following task activation during streaming. A Duration-Scaled Challenge further evaluates these capabilities across four video duration tiers. We develop the Proactive Response Score (PRS) with task-adaptive answer windows to jointly assess answer correctness, response timeliness, historical consistency, and content quality. Extensive experiments and analysis reveal the strengths and limitations of existing models, highlighting directions for advancing proactive streaming video understanding.

input.title: Where Compositionality Hides: Shared-Content Interference in Vision-Language Retrieval
input.comment: 18 pages, 7 figures, 10 tables. Code in ancillary files
input.summary: Paired compositional benchmarks such as Winoground ask each image to prefer its matching caption and each caption to prefer its matching image. A failed Group decision can come from a wrong caption preference or from the cross-image comparison alone, and Group Score merges the two. Choosing between retraining the encoder and changing the scoring rule therefore requires separating them. We study mean-erasure, which projects each frozen image embedding away from the mean of the two normalized candidate captions. We prove that the projection preserves every within-image caption ranking and makes Group Score equal baseline Text Score. On Winoground, mean-erasure raises CLIP ViT-B/32 Group Score from 9% to 31%, and five CLIP and SigLIP checkpoints gain 21 to 27 percentage points. ColorSwap shows a similar gain for color-object binding. A score decomposition shows that about 60% of Image failures already score the correct joint assignment above the swapped one and fail only on an offset between the two images. Fixed corrections and a learned bilinear scorer gain under one point. A direction estimated from retrieved captions gains about five points with two captions and falls below baseline with sixteen. Before retraining an encoder for paired retrieval, measure the Group loss that mean-erasure recovers: gains beyond baseline Text Score require changing the caption decisions themselves.

input.title: REACT: Response-based Expert Assembly from Contextual Trajectories
input.summary: Dense feed-forward networks are unaffected by how their neurons are grouped: every neuron is evaluated. Sparse execution makes this grouping consequential, because each input can access only a few experts. An arbitrary partition can therefore retain pretrained weights while separating computations that an input needs together. We argue that upcycling should organize neurons according to their responses to similar inputs. To establish this correspondence, we introduce a context-guided upcycling approach REACT, Response-based Expert Assembly from Contextual Trajectories, that uses frozen denoising trajectories to connect input contexts with pretrained neuron responses. We first identify contexts after timestep-wise centering to account for distribution shifts across noise levels, then use their associated responses to allocate intact neurons to routed experts. The same contexts initialize the corresponding router entries, aligning expert contents with their intended inputs, while global activation statistics select an always-active shared expert. Layer-wise reconstruction and end-to-end adaptation refine this initialization for sparse execution. On ImageNet-1K, our approach achieves better generation quality while activating only 37.5% of the original FFN parameters and reducing total per-token activated parameters by 27.6%.

input.title: NNS-GS: Non-Local Neural Scattering for Relightable Gaussian Splatting
input.summary: Creating relightable 3D assets of translucent objects is challenging because changing the illumination at one surface location can affect the appearance elsewhere through subsurface scattering. Existing Gaussian-based scattering models typically predict scattering from local features, making this dependence difficult to capture. We present Non-Local Neural Scattering for Gaussian Splatting (NNS-GS), which learns non-local scattering together with geometry-guided local reflection. The scattering module learns how illumination from light-visible surface regions in light space contributes to the shading point in view space, conditioned on regional diffuse responses and spatial relationships. The reflection module supplies these diffuse responses and uses additional geometric guidance to better capture specular highlights and sharp shadow boundaries. To reduce component mixing and support controllable scattering appearance, anchor-based progressive training establishes the diffuse-scattering base before introducing specular reflection and supervises the components separately. Under calibrated point lighting, NNS-GS improves mean PSNR over existing methods by 2.47 dB and 0.81 dB on the synthetic and real translucent scenes, respectively. Additional synthetic comparisons further show that NNS-GS better matches the reference when adjusting scattering attenuation.

input.title: Context-Grounded Skill Internalization for Vision-Language Agents
input.comment: 30 pages, 13 figures, 23 tables, including supplementary material
input.summary: Skill internalization offers a way for agents to learn useful behaviors from skills and use them without explicit guidance in context at inference time. A common approach is to generate demonstration trajectories with the skill in context and then fine-tune the same model on its own trajectories with the skill removed. However, this leads to the problem that the model may learn to reference the removed skill, which we named as context misalignment (CoMi). In this work, we first analyze agent behaviors related to CoMi under this common pipeline. Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ARC-AGI-1, skill-removed fine-tuning consistently results in CoMi: 12.2-46.0% of test trajectories reference the removed skill. To address this problem, we develop Context-Grounded Skill Internalization (CGSI). CGSI uses a sentence detector to identify unsupported references and then masks or rewrites the selected sentences before fine-tuning. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of CGSI and reveal two key findings. (i) Compared with directly fine-tuning with the skill removed, CGSI reduces CoMi at test time by 72.5-94.6% while preserving task success. (ii) Compared with existing reinforcement learning-based skill-internalization baselines, CGSI achieves comparable performance with substantially less training time. CGSI also significantly reduces processing costs compared with large-scale trajectory auditing and correction.

input.title: Differential Proteomics to XAI Rules: A SHAP-FOL-ILP Modeling for Lung Adenocarcinoma
input.summary:
Background: We developed an interpretable workflow linking paired differential proteomics, sparse logistic regression, SHAP attribution, and first-order logic (FOL) rule learning in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD).
  Methods: We analysed 213 CPTAC-LUAD tissue samples (111 tumour, 102 adjacent-normal) from 111 patients, including 102 matched pairs. Protein effect estimation and testing used the same complete pairs, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Sparse logistic regression used five-fold stratified patient-grouped nested cross-validation. Preprocessing and model selection were confined to training data, with feature selection repeated within inner folds. A separate five-fold patient-grouped evaluation tested SHAP-guided inductive logic programming (FOL/ILP) using training-derived evidence and discretisation.
  Results: Quality control retained 9,518 proteins. At FDR below 0.05 and an absolute mean paired log-ratio difference of at least 1, 378 were differentially abundant (40 increased, 338 decreased). The sparse classifier yielded ROC-AUC 0.9997, average precision 0.9998, accuracy 0.9906, and balanced accuracy 0.9906. FOL/ILP yielded held-out accuracy 0.9765, balanced accuracy 0.9767, precision 0.9818, recall 0.9730, and F1 0.9774. HSPA12B, PALM2-AKAP2, STARD13, and PPM1F had non-zero coefficients in all five classifier folds. The most frequent Horn clause occurred in two of five folds. All others occurred once.
  Conclusions: The workflow connects proteomic classification, attribution, and symbolic rules. Performance reflects tumour-versus-adjacent-normal discrimination within one cohort. Biomarker and clinical claims require independent validation, repeated assessment of rule stability, and further biological annotation.

input.title: FASCIA: Seeing Beneath the Surface with Queryable, Personalized Anatomy in Any Pose
input.summary: We present FASCIA (*Functional Anatomical Structures and Composition via Implicit Atlas*), a Momentum Human Rig (MHR)-anchored framework that predicts and poses a person's internal anatomy from their external body shape and skeletal proportions. FASCIA maps a single 290-structure population template onto each individual through a smooth, invertible warp. As people with the same shape can differ internally, a body-dependent Gaussian prior predicts both average warp coordinates and their inter-subject variability. The warp deforms a learned base template into bones, muscles, organs, and fat depots. Extending MHR skinning into the interior enables direct supervision of this model across four automatically labeled CT cohorts and one whole-body MRI cohort. On 82 held-out CT scans, FASCIA reaches a mean volumetric Dice (volume agreement) of 0.48 on named bones and 0.63 on muscles, keeps the majority of bones and muscles in one piece, and yields calibrated voxel probabilities. On 33 held-out whole-body MRI subjects, FASCIA's pointwise field improves tissue overlap over HIT across all compartments, predicts between-person differences in whole-body adipose percentage ($R^2 = 0.88$ vs. $0.38$ in women and $0.54$ vs. $-0.01$ in men), and recovers segment centers of mass within 1.1 mm. Because it needs only an MHR fit, FASCIA can be driven from images, video, or any system that outputs MHR. This opens the door to fitting individualized calibrated musculoskeletal digital twins to video motion data.

input.title: LexiDet-OVD: Benchmarking Lexical Sensitivity in Open-Vocabulary Object Detection
input.summary: Open-vocabulary object detectors localize objects from free-form text prompts, but their reliability depends on how users describe the target. Standard evaluations usually test a fixed class name, leaving prompt-induced failure modes underexplored. We introduce LexiDet-OVD, a benchmark and metric suite for studying lexical sensitivity in open-vocabulary object detection. We organize prompt sets into equivalent, conditional, and broad semantic scopes, and evaluate four detector families on fixed COCO and LVIS samples, each covering 30 classes (800 held-out COCO images and 1,000 LVIS images). Beyond mean and worst-prompt AP50, we report P10, CVaR at 20%, leave-one-prompt-out influence, detection agreement, box consistency, and confidence variance using one-to-one multi-instance matching. Equivalent-prompt best-to-worst gaps range from 5.3 to 23.4 points on COCO1000 and from 5.1 to 29.9 points on LVIS1000-30c, showing that strong average accuracy and lexical stability are distinct properties. We compare maximum-score selection, weighted-box fusion, Prompt Consensus, and an exploratory fusion rule. Aggregation recovers performance in several settings, but no method dominates all model-dataset pairs. A controlled Detic/SHiNe comparison further shows that semantic hierarchy enrichment does not by itself eliminate lexical sensitivity. These results support reporting prompt-distribution robustness alongside conventional open-vocabulary detection accuracy.

input.title: Deterministic Proper Positive-Only Learning Is Independent of ZFC
input.summary: Binary classification from positive-only samples is a variant of PAC learning in which the learner receives i.i.d. samples only from the positive region of an unknown target concept, but is evaluated on the full distribution. Improper learnability in this model has a textbook characterization, whereas proper learnability has remained open for decades. Recent work characterized it for learners with access to randomness, and showed that, unlike in PAC learning, some classes are properly learnable with randomness but not without it, leaving the deterministic case open. We show that this case cannot be resolved within the standard axioms of mathematics (ZFC): there is a class of VC dimension two whose deterministic proper learnability is independent of ZFC, even though a randomized learner provably learns it. Moreover, no dimension of finite character, a desirable property shared by most dimensions in learning theory, characterizes deterministic proper learnability. We also show that the size of the domain is decisive. In ZFC, deterministic proper learnability has a combinatorial characterization on every domain whose cardinality is below a certain threshold, including every countable domain. In contrast, this characterization fails on every domain of sufficiently large cardinality. Under the generalized continuum hypothesis, this threshold is sharp: it is the exact cardinality at which the characterization starts to fail. Finally, our proofs introduce new tools, based on the Erdos--Rado partition theorem, that may be of broader interest.

input.title: Randomized Weighted Distance Nearest Neighbor Classification
input.comment: Writing-polished version of the SMC'26 paper
input.summary: The nearest neighbor classifier is known to be memory-inefficient, and a popular solution is to compress its training data. Recently, a compression algorithm based on weighted distance nearest neighbor (WNN) was proposed, which has elegant theoretical properties and effective classification performance. However, its compression process is computationally expensive, for it performs a greedy search of the densest homogeneous balls in data space. In this paper, we propose a randomized variant RWNN. It simply randomizes the ball search process, and results in substantially reduced compression time (often 0.1%--1% of WNN's) and similar classification accuracy. RWNN also inherits several theoretical properties of WNN including consistency and a generalization bound. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate its efficacy.

input.title: From Learning Rates to Rotational Schedules: Finite-Horizon Theory on the Sphere
input.summary: How should step sizes be scheduled across a finite training horizon? Cosine and warmup-stable-decay (WSD) schedules are widely adopted in large-scale pretraining, yet their effect on optimization also depends on parameter norms. Normalization can make parameter groups scale invariant, so that the loss depends only on their direction, while their norms still affect how fast the parameters rotate. In this work, we formulate schedule design directly in the space of rotational motion. Working within a geodesically convex spherical setting, we derive a last-iterate convergence guarantee for arbitrary rotational schedules that separates their overall scale from their distribution over time. We derive the unique schedule that minimizes this bound and prove that it approaches linear decay as the horizon grows. Empirically, our rotational interpretation and idealized spherical analysis provide useful predictions for LLM pretraining in practice, including schedule comparisons missed by existing analyses. Our analysis predicts schedule ordering across model scales for both vanilla (Adam, Muon) and Hyperball-style (AdamH, MuonH) optimizers. Our Hyperball experiments support the predicted strong performance of linear LR decay and confirm our prediction that WSD underperforms in this setting. Accounting for parameter norm dynamics, we predict instead the strong performance of WSD for Adam and Muon shown in practice. Guided by our theoretical insights, we also derive a new LR schedule for Adam and Muon, which improves over the established cosine and WSD schedules. All in all, these results support the use of rotational dynamics to understand, predict, and ultimately guide scheduling in LLM pretraining.

input.title: GeoFusion: An Uncertain Machine Learning Framework for Sensor Fusion
input.summary: High positioning precision is a critical requirement in many Global Positioning System (GPS) applications, yet achieving it with affordable smartphone sensors remains an open challenge. Existing approaches treat each GPS observation as an absolute point, discarding the uncertainty inherent in the measurement conditions and leaving the cooperative potential of multiple phones observing the same location untapped. In this work, we propose GeoFusion, a three-stage uncertain machine learning framework for cooperative sensor fusion. In the first stage, each GPS observation is modeled as an uncertain object using one of two proposed models: the volcano function, grounded in satellite geometry, and the empirically derived mountain function, built from the statistical structure of real smartphone data. In the second stage, uncertain objects are clustered by location event using partitional and graph-based algorithms. In the third stage, the cluster output is refined using filter-based and learning-based estimators. Experiments on the Google Smartphone Decimeter Challenge dataset show that uncertainty modeling is a primary driver of precision gains: the mountain function significantly outperforms the geometry-only volcano function, and uncertainty-aware UK-medoids significantly outperforms its certain counterpart, k-medoids. A post-clustering deep neural network further refines the cluster estimates, and the recommended configuration achieves a mean absolute error of 2.90 +/- 0.15 meters on held-out test drives, comparable to and on average below the best reported single-phone precision of approximately 3 meters, demonstrating the potential of cooperative uncertainty-aware fusion for affordable GPS sensors.

input.title: FP-Prune: Rethinking Visual Token Pruning from an Information Gain Perspective
input.summary: Visual token pruning can reduce the inference cost of vision language models, but its effectiveness depends on preserving complementary visual information under a limited token budget. A central challenge is to quantify the additional information a candidate token contributes beyond the retained set, a contribution that conventional scores based on attention or similarity struggle to capture directly. In this work, we revisit visual token pruning from the perspective of information gain and use mutual information to characterize the incremental value of candidate tokens. We further establish theoretically that frame potential serves as an effective surrogate for mutual information. Building on this observation, we propose FP-Prune, a training-free visual token pruning method that iteratively removes tokens with low information gain to preserve as much complementary visual information as possible. Experiments on three widely used VLMs and eight datasets demonstrate that FP-Prune outperforms baseline methods in both accuracy and inference efficiency. Further analysis shows that the surrogate objective closely aligns with model performance. Our work provides theoretical grounding and an effective method for visual token pruning.

input.title: Robust Concept Erasure in Text-to-Image Models via Simulating Brain Functional Localization
input.summary: Concept erasure in text-to-image models aims to prevent a target concept from appearing in generated images while preserving general image generation capability. However, erased concepts can still be reactivated by attacks. Prior attacks mainly search text or image input spaces, leaving the initial latent space underexplored. To address this gap, we introduce IVO (Initial latent Variable Optimization), a new concept reactivation attack that changes the starting point of image generation by optimizing the initial latent. Comprehensive experiments across 8 erasure methods show that IVO reactivates erased concepts more effectively than the attack baselines, revealing a blind spot in erasure robustness evaluation. This motivates us to localize model components associated with the target concept and then treat them as intervention sites for more robust concept erasure. We propose CeFlune (Concept Erasure via Functional Localization of Unit Neurons), which adapts brain functional localization to text-to-image models. CeFlune defines linear modules as Unit Neurons and localizes concept-responsive ones by comparing their response trajectories in the model's task and resting states. It then updates the localized Unit Neurons to constrain their responses and the erased model's predictions. Across U-Net diffusion and flow-matching transformer architectures, CeFlune achieves a favorable balance between concept erasure and general image generation capability in comparisons with up to 15 baseline methods. Under IVO and 4 other evaluated attacks, CeFlune also shows lower concept reactivation.

input.title: When Can a Rewiring Control Test LLM Weight Readers? C2 and an Eligibility Protocol
input.summary: Large language models can predict the outputs of small neural networks from raw weights, but success could reflect recognition of weight-space regularities (fingerprints) rather than computation, and function-preserving controls cannot tell these apart. We propose C2, a counterfactual that permutes the columns of a network's final linear readout: every other parameter, and the readout's singular values, norms and entry multiset, are unchanged, and the function can change in an exactly recomputable way; we verify that each evaluated permutation does. C2 separates fingerprinting from computation only under three conditions, which we state as an eligibility protocol: a strategy restricted to C2-invariant summaries must already predict the target; C2 must change a property specific to the rewiring; and the reader's identity must be attested. No natural setting we tested is eligible. On tiny MLPs a frontier reader route followed the rewired function on all 24 networks, but invariant baselines were near chance and its backend could not be attested. In two public CNN zoos the conditions traded off: weight statistics predicted CIFAR-10 accuracy in-distribution, but C2's effect on accuracy was not specific to the swap, while per-image targets were specific but not predictable from invariant summaries. On a constructed population where a planted fingerprint rule works, all conditions hold and C2 separates a rule-following reader from an executor. A self-hosted Qwen3.8-27B followed the rewired function rather than the shortcut, and showed no evidence of using the weights with thinking disabled. A registered replication on fresh networks confirmed both findings (tracking minus stuck 0.875, 95% interval [0.750, 1.000]), and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B also followed the rewiring (tracking minus stuck 0.729 [0.552, 0.885]). The transforms, audits and raw records are available from the authors.

input.title: AgriManager: A Framework and Benchmark for LLM-RL Generalization in Agricultural Management
input.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Track on Evaluations and Datasets
input.summary: Agricultural management is heterogeneous along two axes. The first is distributional shift within a fixed task interface: weather, crops, and prices vary across years and locations while sensors, actions, and objective stay fixed. The second is structural shift across interfaces: different farms expose different observed variables, available actions, and management objectives. We formalize the second axis as schema shift: variation in the policy-facing schema $Σ= (Σ_O, Σ_A, Σ_R)$ between training and deployment. We test whether LLM-RL generalizes across both axes with AgriManager, to our knowledge the first framework that trains LLM policies with RL across multiple process-based crop simulators, unifying DSSAT, WOFOST, and Cycles. We design a three-tier generalization ladder: Tier 1 within-schema distributional shift, Tier 2 single-axis schema shift along $Σ_O / Σ_A / Σ_R$, Tier 3 compositional schema shift across simulators, all scored on a frozen held-out test suite with three training seeds per method. Within fixed schemas, Qwen3-4B trained by RL with explicit reasoning exceeds neural-network PPO trained with the same interaction budget; without reasoning, training stalls near no-action where the reward penalizes input use. Under single-axis schema shift, $Σ_O$ transfer needs decision-critical state, $Σ_A$ results are consistent with joint action-menu coverage, and with reasoning a policy trained on yield alone transfers to unseen objectives. Under compositional schema shift, single-source training mostly hurts zero-shot transfer across simulators, and a unified policy trained only on other combinations of the same components recovers about 86% of the gain of a specialist trained on the target combination on DSSAT and stays below the specialists on the WOFOST and Cycles profit targets. Project page: https://agrimanager-framework.github.io

input.title: Aegis: A Conversational Prototype for Lung Cancer Risk Information and Follow-up
input.comment: 30 pages, including 12 pages of main text and references and 18 pages of supplementary material; 27 references. All authors contributed equally and share first authorship
input.summary: Collecting self-reported risk information and maintaining continuity between assessment, explanation, and follow-up are practical components of a lung cancer screening workflow. We present Aegis, a browser-based research prototype that combines a conversational questionnaire, rule-based risk categorization, downloadable reports, retrieval-augmented health information, and doctor-user communication. A session-oriented controller manages question progression and clarification, while a language model assists with answer validation. Structured responses are passed to a separate risk-analysis module, and reports are linked to user and session records through Firebase services. The project adopts a multi-agent design that separates information collection, validation, assessment, and report generation. Its documented verification scope comprises 45 functional test specifications covering account management, questionnaire interaction, reporting, doctor-side review, and consultation. The available evaluation describes workflow behavior qualitatively; it provides no per-case execution results, clinical cohort, predictive-performance measurements, or comparative experiments. We therefore present Aegis as an engineering prototype for organizing risk information and follow-up, with clinical validity and the benefits of its agent-based design remaining unestablished. The paper describes the implementation, distinguishes implemented workflows from incomplete extensions, and identifies the evidence required for reproducible and clinically meaningful evaluation.

input.title: CLASP: Deciding Structure and Claims Before Decoding for Whole-Slide Pathology Report Generation
input.summary: Whole-slide pathology report generation has advanced through stronger slide encoders, retrieved knowledge, and, recently, slide-level multimodal LLMs. However, these generators leave every report-level choice to the decoder: how long the report is, how it is organised, and which findings it states and where. On the standard PathText-BRCA benchmark, we find that these choices dominate n-gram overlap, as reports from the query's hospital selected without learning approach the state of the art, while decoders under-generate and fall back to the most frequent findings. We present CLASP, a decide-then-decode generator that makes these choices explicitly, once per slide. Before decoding, an Exemplar Structure Prior (ESP) takes the sentence plan and length from reports of image-similar cases, a Calibrated Claim Decision (CCD) selects the findings from calibrated slide posteriors, and a Claim-to-Sentence Placement (CSP) assigns each finding to a planned sentence. A Plan-Conditioned Decoder (PCD), refined by structure-anchored sequence training, then writes the report under these decisions. With 35M parameters, CLASP outperforms retrained report generators and slide-level LLMs of up to 7B parameters, matches the strongest published results, and generalises to lung cancer from unseen hospitals. Its decisions change what the reports state, not only their length, transfer to an LLM decoder, and can withhold what H&E cannot show: withholding receptor status leaves 23% fewer contradictions with clinical records than the same network without decisions.

input.title: ESM-Bench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Whether AI Agents Understand Earth System Model Physics and Code
input.summary: AI coding agents that modify Earth System Model (ESM) code must preserve both software interfaces and the physical assumptions encoded in them. We introduce ESM-Bench, a benchmark of 60 developer-commit tasks from 6 repositories: Noah-MP, CLM5, SUMMA, ParFlow, MOM6, and VIC. The v5 corpus contains 17 physics-based bug fixes, 16 process-representation modifications, 13 parameterization-scheme selections, and 14 parameter-optimization tasks. Each task includes a scientific objective, parent-commit source files, a reference diff, and three stored prompt variants. An artifact audit confirms that all 60 reference diffs apply to their supplied starting files. We define an eight-item patch-review rubric and audit five archived patch fixtures against the implemented local checkers. None of the five fixture diffs applies to its supplied starting files, yet three text-pattern checkers return a pass. A ParFlow expression replay disagrees with the reference slopes, and a MOM6 pattern check detects an omitted update. Inspection also identifies a retained VIC reference assignment that overwrites the intended vegetation-specific albedo. These findings expose limits of reference patches and local proxies as correctness evidence. The release provides a reproducible corpus and diagnostic tools; complete expert validation, comparative agent performance, and full-model execution remain unmeasured on v5.

input.title: Center-Aware Ordinal Learning for Prostate Cancer Grading from Histopathology Images
input.comment: 6 pages, 3 figures. Accepted as an oral presentation at SPIE Medical Imaging 2027
input.summary: Prostate cancer grading from histopathology whole-slide images (WSIs) is complicated by the ordered nature of ISUP grades, class imbalance, and center-dependent variations in staining, tissue preparation, and scanning. Most weakly supervised methods treat grade groups as independent categories and may therefore learn representations that do not transfer reliably across institutions. We propose a center-aware ordinal learning framework that combines a pretrained pathology encoder with attention-based multiple instance learning. The framework uses an Earth Mover's Distance loss to account for ordinal errors, an ordinal supervised contrastive objective to align same-grade slides across centers while separating grades according to disease severity, and curriculum learning to reduce the dominance of benign cases. We evaluate the framework on approximately 9,100 biopsy WSIs from the two-center PANDA dataset. The proposed framework achieves an accuracy of 0.842 and a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.958 on the held-out test set. Its main benefit is observed in cross-center transfer: when a linear probe is trained on Karolinska representations and evaluated on Radboud, accuracy increases from 0.643 to 0.823 and quadratic weighted kappa from 0.899 to 0.930. Performance remains stable in the reverse direction. UMAP projections further show improved mixing between centers while preserving an ordinal grade trajectory. These results suggest that combining ordinal and center-aware objectives produces more transferable slide representations for multi-center prostate cancer grading.

input.title: FinEvo: Recursive Self-Improvement for Long-Horizon Financial Modeling
input.summary: Advances in large language models (LLMs) have expanded their role in high-value productivity tasks, including financial analysis and modeling, while enabling models to play an increasingly active role in their own improvement. This motivates two complementary lines of inquiry: can financial modeling capabilities provide a foundation for model self-evolution, and can self-evolution, in turn, advance financial capabilities? We introduce FinEvo, a self-evolution framework that integrates autonomous experience construction with financial capability improvement. FinEvo prepares financial models, iteratively evolves challenges through self-play, and learns from the resulting interactions using executable rewards, relying on the same model throughout. An end-to-end execution with Qwen3.6-27B shows that solving feedback supports both increasing reasoning demands and identifying specification issues that executable checks can miss. Learning from these experiences raises whole-task success from 22.73 to 29.09 on held-out within-source tasks and from 13.13 to 19.19 on SpreadsheetBench 2 Financial. Comparable gains across task sources and evaluation settings, together with improvement on a task category absent from training, suggest that FinEvo strengthens underlying financial modeling capabilities shared across tasks. These findings support self-evolution as a path toward broader financial competence, advancing the empirical exploration of recursive self-improvement (RSI) in professional domains. Code is available at https://github.com/pcj-sudo/FinEvo.

input.title: torchtsetlin: Fast, Interpretable Tsetlin Machines for PyTorch
input.summary: The Tsetlin machine learns propositional rules with teams of Tsetlin automata that are driven by reward and penalty rather than gradients, so its models are interpretable by construction and cheap to evaluate. Its software, however, consists of C and CUDA kernels behind scikit-learn-style wrappers that sit outside the deep learning ecosystem. torchtsetlin implements the Tsetlin machine family as ordinary PyTorch modules: vanilla and weighted, coalesced, regression, convolutional over sequences, images and volumes, and dense per-pixel segmentation. The automata are a tensor buffer, so a model moves with .to(device), is saved with state_dict() and learns from a mini-batch with one update(x,y) call. Its core technique is a batched formulation of Type I and Type II feedback, in which automaton transitions become event counts realised as binomial draws, with one commit per mini-batch. On ten benchmarks taken from the existing libraries, it matches their accuracy, and on all but the two smallest it trains 2.4-10.9X faster than PyTsetlinMachineCUDA and 10.3-81.2X faster than tmu on the same GPU. The package is pure Python, MIT-licensed and on PyPI; every number in this paper is reproduced by one script. Code: https://github.com/vlbthambawita/torchtsetlin; package: https://pypi.org/project/torchtsetlin/.

input.title: PhoneQC: Benchmarking Multimodal LLMs for Order-Level Smartphone Trade-in Inspection
input.summary: As vision-language models enter remote smartphone trade-in, sellers already upload six views and a diagnostic screen, which makes it easy to treat the human quote as a step a model can take over. A model may mark a crack or read the screen, yet the quote is a staff form: appearance fill stays near 0.25, and the closed models that score a little higher do so only on the orders they answer, so human appraisal remains necessary. Two obstacles stand in the way. (1) Single-view defect sets and attribute benchmarks do not score an order-level form under a fixed input contract, so a box or a leaked field can be mistaken for a finished quote. (2) The unread half of the form is the staff fields, and a model left to emit boxes or captions does not learn them. We present PhoneQC, a 335-order iPhone-heavy cut that ranks systems by a 0 to 100 form score (Score100) only inside matched protocols (images alone; images plus a detector sidecar), with a declared upper bound that is not ranked as a peer. As a case study on that board, field-only LoRA freezes the backbone, adapts attention projections, and supervises staff fields while leaving the defect list empty; the adapter sees the same images as the zero-shot model. On image-only T1 the 3B model rises from 26.6 to 33.3 at coverage 0.928; without the empty-blocker item the open ranking still favors the adapter, while the remaining gap to a person stays large on this cut.

input.title: Tangent incompleteness under coupled image transformations: margin reconstruction and decision consequences
input.summary: Can accurate responses to individual geometric image transformations recover their combined effect on a classifier's decision? For identity-aligned bilinear resampling, coordinatewise assembly may fail at first order. Projecting the implemented transformation onto a fixed logit-margin gradient, we derive a linear term plus signed absolute-value ridges. An exact even--odd identity and ridge-cancellation conditions characterize the missing information. Under independent parameter laws, a noncancelling off-coordinate ridge obstructs even unrestricted additive fits. The coupled correction has $O(s^2)$ projected error, versus a possible $Θ(s)$ axiswise defect; transfer to realized network margins requires local smoothness. Projected RMS errors fall by 82.96% on CIFAR-10 and 82.38% on ImageNetV2 relative to axiswise assembly; realized fixed-pair margin RMS errors fall by 39.75% and 42.73%. The representation prospectively identifies nine strict nonadditive network-margin sign configurations and permits exact minimization of a three-parameter threat surrogate, with conditional selection-regret guarantees. In an independent CIFAR-10 search, coupled-selected transformations uncover 51 top-1 changes versus 41 for axes. On 256 independent ImageNetV2/ConvNeXt-Tiny images and 16,384 transformed decisions at the prespecified scale $s=.40$, multiclass top-1 flip-prediction errors fall from 11.97% to 10.23% (paired improvement 1.74 percentage points; 95% interval [0.93, 2.61]). Directional finite differences are slightly more accurate (10.00%) at higher measured model-construction cost. These results connect first-order sampling interactions to margin reconstruction, decision prediction, and threat selection, without claiming finite-scale network certification.

input.title: LightOnOCR for AMNLT: Reading Chant Notation and Lyrics in One Pass, from Single Staves to Whole Pages
input.summary: Aligned music notation and lyrics transcription (AMNLT) asks for the notes of a chant, its sung text and the assignment of syllables to notes in one output. Fuentes-Martínez et al., who defined the task, found that the one vision-language model they tested fell far behind specialised recognisers. We fine-tune LightOnOCR-3-1B, a page OCR model with one billion parameters, end to end, vision encoder included, to write a staff as a GABC string whose letters denote staff positions. Trained on the published AMNLT training split alone, it more than halves the best published aligned music and lyrics error rate (AMLER) on Solesmes, the one directly comparable dataset (9.9 against 21.0 %); on Einsiedeln and Salzinnes, measured in a different encoding, its figures are also lower. The benchmark does not measure generalisation to unseen manuscripts: while the pitch error on AMNLT validation stays between 1.7 and 1.9 %, on 200 staves from five unseen manuscripts it falls from 24.9 to 1.3 % as we add chant aligned through CantusDB, Transkribus ground truth and silver staves kept only where two readers agree. Trained also on multi-staff images, it reads whole pages without staff detection (pitch error 3.3 to 3.8 % on validation and test pages, 1.9 % on pages of unseen manuscripts). Remaining errors include Gothic F clefs read as C clefs, notes dropped with abbreviated or illegible text and lower accuracy on pages with small notation. Controlled ablations are needed to explain the gains.
